ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Programmatic cue-grounding benchmark for audiovisual emotion reasoning
PROPOSAL: Assemble a benchmark from MAFW and DFEW clips in which annotators list the audio and visual cues that truly explain each emotion, plus distractor cues such as clothing color and room noise. Score a model response with a deterministic matcher that maps stated cues to the annotated list, giving a reasoning-error rate for distractor cues and a perception-error rate for cues absent from the clip. No external LLM judge is called. Evaluate Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, video-SALMONN 2 and EmoVIT on the full pool in one pass each.
CONTROLS: Compare the matcher against human judgments on a 200-response sample; include a keyword-overlap scorer and a random-cue scorer as baselines; ablate the synonym lexicon used for matching.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Matcher agreement with humans should exceed 0.85 Cohen kappa and rank models consistently. It could fail for paraphrased cues the lexicon misses, which would understate perception errors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reproducible cue scoring set for audiovisual emotion reasoning
PROPOSAL: Build a scoring set from MAFW and DFEW clips where annotators write the cues that explain each emotion and mark distractors. Each clip is annotated by three annotators in two rounds with adjudication, and a second pool is drawn from CAER-S and MER2023 and annotated the same way. A rule-based matcher turns stated cues into reasoning-error and perception-error rates without any external judge. Evaluate Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and video-SALMONN 2 once on the pool.
CONTROLS: Check the matcher against human judgments on a 100-response sample; use a keyword-overlap scorer as baseline; ablate the synonym lexicon; report annotator agreement per round.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: The matcher should reach about 0.85 kappa with humans and order the models stably. A failure would come from paraphrases the lexicon misses, which would understate perception errors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Preference tuning against invented cues with synthetic negatives
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with direct preference optimization on pairs built from MAFW clips: the preferred response cites only cues verified by Whisper transcripts and OpenFace action units, while the rejected response is the same text with one fabricated cue inserted, for example tears matched to crying audio that is absent. Train with LoRA rank 16 on 6000 pairs for one epoch and evaluate on held-out clips for cue-level precision and recall, emotion accuracy and keyword F1.
CONTROLS: Compare with supervised fine-tuning on the preferred responses alone, a model trained on randomly paired responses, and the untuned model; ablate the fabricated-cue insertion rate.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: Cue precision should rise by several points over supervised tuning with emotion accuracy within one point. It could fail if fabricated cues are too easy to spot, so the policy learns surface edits only.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tuning an audiovisual model against inserted cues with controlled negatives
PROPOSAL: Train Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with direct preference optimization on pairs from MAFW clips: preferred responses cite only cues verified by Whisper transcripts and OpenFace action units, rejected ones add a single invented cue. Use LoRA rank 16 on 6000 pairs, and rerun the identical recipe on DFEW, CAER-S and MER2023 clips with its own pair set, with checkpoints saved at intervals of 200 steps and each scored on cue precision, cue recall, emotion accuracy and keyword F1.
CONTROLS: Compare with supervised fine-tuning on preferred responses only, random pairing, and the untuned model; ablate the insertion rate and the pair filter threshold.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: Cue precision should rise over supervised tuning with accuracy preserved. It could fail if inserted cues are trivially detectable, so the model learns surface edits and checkpoints show no trend.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modality-contrastive decoding to suppress language-prior cues
PROPOSAL: At inference, contrast the logits of the full audiovisual input against a branch where the video frames are replaced by a blank clip and a branch where the audio is replaced by silence, down-weighting tokens that survive when evidence is removed. Apply it to Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and video-SALMONN 2 on EMER and MAFW, and tune the contrast weight on a development split of 300 clips. Measure perception-error rate with a cue-existence checker built on audio tagging and a vision captioner, and emotion accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare with greedy decoding, nucleus sampling and a text-only contrast branch; ablate each removed modality separately; test on clips where tears and sobbing both occur.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: Perception errors should fall by about a fifth at a small accuracy cost. It could fail when the language prior and true cues coincide, because contrast would suppress valid cues too.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrastive decoding over audio and video to reduce prior-driven cues
PROPOSAL: Contrast logits of the full audiovisual input with a branch showing blank frames and a branch with silent audio, so that tokens persisting without evidence are down-weighted. Apply it to Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, video-SALMONN 2, EmotionLLaMA and AffectGPT on EMER, MAFW, DFEW and MER2023, tuning the contrast weight over a grid of 12 values on each dataset separately with 300 development clips. Measure perception-error rate with a checker built on audio tagging and a vision captioner, plus emotion accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare with greedy decoding and nucleus sampling; ablate each removed modality separately; report the gain at each tuned weight in a table.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: Perception errors should drop around a fifth at a small accuracy cost. It may fail where the prior coincides with real cues, since contrast and removes valid cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cue-removal probes of grounding in audiovisual emotion models
PROPOSAL: Probe whether predictions depend on the cues that explain them. For 400 MAFW clips with annotated cues, remove one annotated cue at a time by masking the face region or filtering the vocal band, and measure how the emotion keyword distribution of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B shifts. Compare with removing a distractor cue of equal duration. A grounded model should move more under explanatory removals than under distractor removals.
CONTROLS: Control for masking artifacts with a blurred-but-informative mask; compare against a random-segment removal; use two seeds for mask placement.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Explanatory removal should shift predictions at least twice as much as distractor removal for a grounded model. It could fail if masks introduce distribution shift that dominates the effect.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cue-removal probes with attention rollouts for emotion models
PROPOSAL: Probe whether predictions depend on explanatory cues. For 400 MAFW clips with annotated cues, remove cues by masking the face region or filtering the vocal band, and track how the keyword distribution of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B shifts, comparing with removal of a distractor of equal duration. Then repeat on 1500 clips from DFEW, MER2023 and CAER-S, combine each removal type pairwise, and compute attention rollouts per variant and per clip, averaged over layers.
CONTROLS: Control for mask artifacts with a blurred mask; compare with random-segment removal; use two seeds for mask placement; report rollout agreement per variant.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Explanatory removal should shift predictions more than distractor removal. It could fail if mask artifacts dominate, and rollouts may track position rather than cue identity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Verified instruction data from audiovisual detectors for emotion descriptions
PROPOSAL: Construct instruction data for emotion descriptions by drafting captions with a 7B MLLM and keeping only sentences whose cues are confirmed by independent detectors: Whisper for speech content, a sound-event tagger for ambient audio, OpenFace for facial action units and a pose estimator for gestures. Build 20000 verified samples from VoxCeleb2 and MELD, fine-tune Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with LoRA and evaluate cue precision, emotion accuracy and a reasoning-error rate on a held-out benchmark.
CONTROLS: Compare with unfiltered captions, filtering by a single detector, and filtering by a proprietary judge; ablate each detector in turn; test the verifier recall on 150 hand-checked sentences.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Verified data should lower perception errors relative to unfiltered captions with the same sample count. It could fail if detector gaps discard valid cues and thin the data toward easy emotions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Instruction data for emotion descriptions filtered by detector agreement
PROPOSAL: Draft emotion descriptions with a 7B MLLM and keep only sentences whose cues are confirmed by Whisper, a sound-event tagger, OpenFace action units and a pose estimator. Build verified sets of 20000 samples from VoxCeleb2 and MELD, and further sets of 20000 from MAFW, DFEW and MER2023, and fine-tune Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with LoRA on each set and on their union, and evaluate cue precision, emotion accuracy and a reasoning-error rate on a held-out benchmark after each epoch.
CONTROLS: Compare with unfiltered captions and single-detector filtering; ablate each detector; test verifier recall on 150 hand-checked sentences.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Verified sets should cut perception errors relative to unfiltered captions at equal sample count. It may fail if detector gaps discard valid cues and skew data toward easy emotions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention-mass regularizer tying emotion tokens to annotated cue segments
PROPOSAL: Add a training loss that rewards attention mass from emotion keyword tokens onto audio and video tokens inside annotated cue segments of MAFW clips, with a penalty for mass on distractor segments. Fine-tune Qwen2.5-Omni-7B for 2 epochs with LoRA and select the loss weight on a development split. Report emotion accuracy, cue-level precision and attention-to-cue ratio on EMER.
CONTROLS: Compare with plain fine-tuning, a regularizer using random segments, and one using uniform attention targets; ablate the distractor penalty; check layer choice for the attention readout.
COST: 1100
PREDICTION: Attention-to-cue ratio should rise by half with accuracy unchanged. It could fail if attention is a poor proxy of reliance, which would raise the ratio without reducing invented cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention-mass regularizer tying emotion tokens to annotated cue segments in five corpora
PROPOSAL: Add a loss that rewards attention from emotion keyword tokens onto tokens inside annotated cue segments, penalizing mass on distractor segments. Fine-tune Qwen2.5-Omni-7B for 2 epochs with LoRA on MAFW, and run the same recipe on DFEW, MER2023, CAER-S and MELD each with a loss weight chosen from 20 values on its own development split. Report emotion accuracy, cue precision and the ratio of attention on cue segments on EMER at each layer.
CONTROLS: Compare with plain fine-tuning and a regularizer using random segments; ablate the distractor penalty; log the readout at each layer.
COST: 1100
PREDICTION: The ratio should rise substantially with accuracy unchanged. It could fail if attention is a weak proxy of reliance, raising the ratio without lowering invented cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Counterfactual audio swaps to measure spurious cue-emotion links
PROPOSAL: Build counterfactual clips by swapping audio tracks between MAFW videos whose emotions differ, such as laughter placed over a crying face. Ask Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and video-SALMONN 2 to describe the emotion and its cues, and test whether stated cues follow the swapped audio or the typical co-occurrence. Score with a cue-existence checker and report the rate of cues invented from priors on 300 swapped clips.
CONTROLS: Include unswapped controls from the same speakers, swaps between same-emotion clips, and a model with the audio stream removed; vary the loudness match between tracks.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Invented cue rates should be higher on conflicting swaps than on same-emotion swaps. It could fail if models simply attend to the face and ignore sound in both conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Counterfactual audio and video swaps to measure cue-emotion links
PROPOSAL: Build counterfactual clips by swapping audio tracks between MAFW videos of differing emotion, such as laughter over a crying face, and by swapping video between speakers of MELD and MER2023. Ask Qwen2.5-Omni-7B and video-SALMONN 2 to describe the emotion and its cues and test whether stated cues follow the swapped audio or the typical pairing. Score with a cue-existence checker on 300 conflicting swaps, and on 3000 swaps drawn from each emotion pair.
CONTROLS: Include unswapped controls from the same speakers and swaps between same-emotion clips; vary loudness match; report each emotion pair separately.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Invented cue rates should be higher for conflicting swaps than same-emotion swaps. It could fail if models rely on the face and ignore sound in both conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Verifier-reward reinforcement learning for cue-faithful emotion reasoning
PROPOSAL: Train Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with a GRPO-style objective whose reward combines emotion keyword match and a cue-faithfulness score computed by programmatic checkers: a stated audio cue must be confirmed by a sound-event tagger and a stated visual cue by a face and scene detector. Sample 8 responses per clip from 5000 MAFW clips, train for 400 steps, and evaluate on EMER and a held-out benchmark for perception errors, reasoning errors and accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare with reward on keyword match alone, supervised tuning on the same clips, and a reward using a proprietary judge on a subset; ablate the faithfulness weight; check reward gaming by verifier-evasive phrasing.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: Perception errors should drop by a third relative to keyword-only reward. It could fail if the model learns to state fewer cues, which raises faithfulness scores at the cost of detail.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Verifier-reward policy optimization for cue-faithful emotion descriptions
PROPOSAL: Train Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with a group-relative objective whose reward mixes emotion keyword match and a faithfulness score from programmatic checkers: stated audio cues must be confirmed by a sound-event tagger and stated visual cues by a face and scene detector. Sample 8 responses per clip from 5000 MAFW clips and repeat the run with the 14B variant, and with three reward mixing weights per model and 4 sampling temperatures, evaluating on EMER for perception errors, reasoning errors and accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare with keyword-only reward and supervised tuning on the same clips; ablate the faithfulness weight; check gaming by evasive phrasing in each run.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: Perception errors should drop relative to keyword-only reward. It may fail if the policy learns to state fewer cues, raising faithfulness at the cost of detail.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cue-level abstention and calibration for audiovisual emotion explanations
PROPOSAL: Train a lightweight head on the final-layer representation of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B that predicts, for each cue the model states, whether that cue is present in the clip, using cue labels from MAFW and EMER. Use its output to drop or flag low-confidence cues before presenting the response. Report cue precision at fixed recall, expected calibration error and emotion accuracy on held-out clips.
CONTROLS: Compare with the model's own token probabilities, a head trained on shuffled labels, and a text-only head that sees the cue words without the clip; ablate the layer used for features.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: The head should beat token probability on precision at 0.8 recall by several points. It could fail because a cue's presence is hard to read from a late layer, leaving only language-prior signal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cue-level abstention and calibration with heads at many layers
PROPOSAL: Train lightweight heads on the representations of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B that predict, for each stated cue, whether the cue is present in the clip, using cue labels from MAFW and EMER. Train one head per layer, per modality pooling choice and per seed, and use the best combination to flag low-confidence cues. Report cue precision at fixed recall, expected calibration error and emotion accuracy on held-out clips from each head.
CONTROLS: Compare with the model's token probabilities, a head trained on shuffled labels, and a text-only head; report the layer-wise curves by pooling choice.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: The best head should beat token probability on precision at fixed recall. It could fail because presence is hard to read out of late layers, leaving only prior signal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Open-vocabulary emotion keyword scoring with a local embedding matcher
PROPOSAL: Replace the two-stage proprietary-judge pipeline with a local scorer for open-vocabulary emotion keywords. Map predicted and reference keywords into the embedding space of a sentence encoder, match them by optimal assignment with a similarity threshold tuned on a development split of EMER, and report precision, recall and F1. Score the outputs of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, EmotionLLaMA and AffectGPT on 500 clips and compare the resulting model ranking with a published judge-based ranking.
CONTROLS: Compare with exact string match, WordNet synonym expansion and a lemmatized overlap baseline; ablate the threshold; test stability across two sentence encoders.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Ranking correlation with the judge-based ordering should exceed 0.9 Spearman. It could fail for rare keywords whose neighbors in embedding space are other emotions of opposite valence.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Open-vocabulary emotion keyword scoring with local embedding matchers and thresholds
PROPOSAL: Replace the two-stage proprietary-judge pipeline with local scorers for open-vocabulary emotion keywords. Map predicted and reference keywords into sentence-encoder embeddings, match them by optimal assignment with a similarity threshold tuned on EMER development clips, and report precision, recall and F1. Repeat with 3 encoders and 4 thresholds, scoring Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, EmotionLLaMA and AffectGPT on 500 clips and comparing each ranking with a published judge-based ranking.
CONTROLS: Compare with exact string match and a lemmatized overlap baseline; ablate the threshold; report rank stability across encoders.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Ranking correlation with the judge-based ordering should be high. It could fail for rare keywords whose embedding neighbors are emotions of opposite valence.
